item.title: Ordering violence from abroad: five suspects arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France
item.description:
Five suspects linked to the organisation and recruitment of serious violence have been arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France, in the latest results of the Operational Taskforce (OTF) GRIMM, coordinated by Europol.
The arrests in August and September target the upper levels of violence-as-a-service: those suspected of ordering attacks, finding perpetrators and coordinating crimes from abroad. Among those apprehended are fugitives featured on the EU Most Wanted website.

item.title: No click required: How the ad industry became a pipeline for mercenary spyware
item.description:
That ad you just scrolled past on your phone but barely spared a look or click? It could be tracking your movements and collecting your data, without you having to do a thing.

This “zero-click mercenary spyware,” dubbed “AdFection,” is increasingly exploiting a sprawling online advertising ecosystem ripe for abuse, according to researchers at The Citizen Lab. One top actor in the space, Discover-Tech, runs the Controlium platform that allows cyber criminals to “precisely profile and de-anonymize” millions of users, fingerprint them, and automatically infect their devices when an ad is displayed.

Troublingly, Discover-Tech is successfully masquerading as a legitimate ad company across the online ad sales environment, the researchers said, listed as a “certified” and “approved” vendor by the likes of Google and IAB Europe.

Over a four-month period, the company’s ads were shown on nearly 200,000 unique websites and in Android/iOS apps in dozens of countries. Furthermore, its ads have been presented through major networks like Google, Yandex, and Beeswax, and it even exploited the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) consent frameworks to target victims in the EU.

The Citizen Lab researchers disclosed their findings to Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle (Liftoff), and Eskimi, all of whom took action to disconnect Discover-Tech’s access to the digital advertising ecosystem.

“Discover-Tech’s mass abuse, privacy invasion, and facilitation for mercenary spyware attacks illustrates structural flaws with the online advertising system, which failed to detect or prevent the abuse,” the researchers warned.

How AdFection exploits a largely unprotected system

The online ad market operates largely via real-time bidding (RTB), auctions hosted by ad exchanges. Run by companies like Google, these take place “hundreds of billions” times a day, the researchers explained. When an ad box pops up on an app or website on a user’s device, it immediately triggers a bid request; advertisers then submit their offers, and the exchange grants a winner the ability to push their ad to the user within split seconds. These ads can contain images, video, and, most importantly to cybercriminals, code.

Demand-side platforms (DSPs) and supply-side platforms (SSPs) act as intermediaries in the process, and data about specific users and devices is shared across the exchanges so advertisers can decide whether they want to show specific ads to a specific individual, based on device identifiers and characteristics such as a user’s precise location, cookie ID, mobile ad ID, or IP address.

“The auction system is designed to enable targeting single individuals,” the researchers explained. “The totality of information gleaned from ad auctions is quite valuable.” Companies with access to auction data can track users without their knowledge, across cellular, Wi-Fi, and virtual private networks (VPNs).

Discover-Tech has effectively infiltrated and connected the spyware industry to this online ecosystem, which includes infamous Israeli mercenary spyware vendor Candiru. Its partners can deliver ads to “mass-profile unwitting phone users,” and silently infect the devices of select targets, according to the researchers.

When Discover-Tech wins a bid, one of its ads is pushed to a website or app that is open on a user’s device. Sometimes this is seen by the user; other times is merely renders in the background.

Many of these ads have been shown to devices on national security-sensitive networks, in security organizations including NATO, networks associated with critical infrastructure, and media organizations around the world. Using AdFection, Candiru’s spyware infected devices at international news network Al Jazeera.

The researchers emphasized that a Discover-Tech ad impression does not mean that a device has been infected with spyware. However, the fact that the company has been able to bid on and show ads across sprawling ad networks highlights a “systemic risk” warranting “urgent investigation.”

Lack of vetting

Discover-Tech’s ads carried no exploit at all, noted Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “The ad was clean; that is the frightening part. Nobody clicked anything.”

Instead, each ad called home with the device’s advertising ID and IP address. In almost every case, the server sent back nothing, Dickson emphasized; only chosen targets received malicious code.

“Third-party verification scanners saw a harmless banner, because for nearly every viewer, it was one,” he said. This is exactly how tags slipped past verification.

Also alarming is the reach: Discover-Tech’s ads displayed in 75,373 apps and 120,768 websites over the course of four months, and had impressions on networks belonging to NATO, Intel, Microsoft, and Apple. While the report emphasizes that an impression is not an infection, the company’s targeting clearly reached enterprise networks, Dickson said.

Just as troublingly is the badge: Discover-Tech was listed as a certified or approved vendor for years. The report said that vetting often amounted to self-attestation, a box checked on a form. “A certification is only as good as the vetting behind it,” Dickson said.

Steps enterprises should take now

On managed browsers, ad blockers are necessary, but they’re not wholly sufficient, Dickson said. Many Discover-Tech bids were for ads inside mobile apps, typically overlooked by browser extensions. But clearly, desktops are at play too; Candiru targeted Al Jazeera’s Windows software.

Dickson advised enterprises to:

  • Push a vetted ad-blocking extension to managed browsers through policy rather than leaving it to users to install it.
  • Favor browsers with built-in tracking protection.
  • Block ad and tracking domains at the DNS or secure web gateway layer; this reaches in-app ads on managed phones.
  • Disable advertising identifiers on corporate mobile devices through mobile device management (MDM) and restrict ad-supported consumer apps on devices holding sensitive data.
  • Turn on Apple’s Lockdown Mode for high-risk executives, journalists, and any users traveling to sensitive locations.
  • Keep browsers and operating systems patched “The ad is only the delivery truck; the exploit still needs a flaw,” he pointed out.
  • Watch traffic tied to ad impressions for odd follow-on requests.
  • Finally, search domain name system (DNS) and proxy logs for the domains published in the report.

The advertising ID in particular deserves a hard look, Dickson pointed out. The Citizen Lab report says that blocking advertising identifiers alone would have stopped this attack method.

Troublingly, he noted, many enterprises spend fortunes managing their users’ identities, then let corporate phones hand that persistent identifier to anonymous auctions that run hundreds of billions of times a day.

“Every ad is someone else’s code running on your device,” Dickson said. “Treat the ad network like any other untrusted vendor.”

item.title: Malware evasion made easier with AI — but behavior still gives it away
item.description:
Fresh research suggests recent panic over AI-generated malware may be overblown.

Last month Anthropic detailed how Russia-linked cyberespionage group Midnight Blizzard used Claude to rebuild malware each time security tools flagged its backdoor as malign.

“We observed GTG-20006 operate through customized AI-driven workflows that automated much of their operations from development, infrastructure acquisition, phishing, persistence through command and control, to data exfiltration,” the AI company wrote in its report, referring to Midnight Blizzard, aka APT29 and Cozy Bear, as GTG-20006.

While the group’s use of AI as part of its operations is notable, what raised eyebrows was how it did so as part of its evasion strategy: “If their monitoring AI agents identified that any of their deployed malware was detected by a security product, agents would then set about the process of autonomously modifying and rebuilding the malware to evade the existing detections. The agents were designed to continue iterating on GTG-20006’s toolkit until it was undetected,” Anthropic reported.

That autonomous loop — from monitoring for detection to rebuilding the malware to fine-tune evasion — raises the spectre of polymorphic AI malware, malicious software that changes its code structure automatically while keeping the same core functionality.

But threat intelligence company ReversingLabs (RL) has since released a report detailing how its telemetry and behavior-based threat hunting flagged the campaign’s Go backdoor PowerShell stager as malicious on Aug. 1, weeks before Anthropic’s Sept. 10 report.

RL subsequently saw five versions of the same stager over the course of 25 days. Although each had a different hash, all five behaved the same way. That consistent behavior profile left each iteration open to detection, according to a technical blog post by ReversingLabs published last week, as analysts could still hunt for what the malware did and how its files and infrastructure were connected.

As a result, evasion via AI rebuilds may not yet be as foolproof as first feared.

Variations on a well-worn theme

Changing a file to dodge detection is one of the oldest techniques in the business, and polymorphic malware has been deployed to dodge signatures for decades.

“What stands out with this Midnight Blizzard activity is outsourcing the busywork to an LLM,” says Ben Bernstein, manager of the cybersecurity advisors team at managed detection and response firm Huntress. “They wired an AI agent to monitor security tools and automatically generate fresh variants without human intervention. We have seen basic script automation do this, but large language models just make the refactoring cleaner and faster.”

Huntress backs ReversingLabs’ argument that while AI makes malware faster to rebuild it fails to change the hallmarks of its malicious behavior.

“Models are fantastic at scrambling code structure and swapping variables to bypass static analysis,” says Bernstein. “But the AI is not inventing novel exploits. It just automates the grunt work of rewriting the same script to ensure the file hashes change.”

In short, Bernstein says, “the packaging looks different, but the payload’s core objective remains exactly the same.”

Malicious experiments in AI-assisted malware development

Still, AI-assisted malware rebuilding is an emerging if not unprecedented tactic among malware developers.

For example, Google documented PromptFlux in late 2025, an experimental script that asked Gemini to rewrite its own source every hour, and PromptSteal, which APT28 used against Ukraine to generate commands at runtime.

In March 2026, Microsoft released a report describing how the North Korean cluster Coral Sleet is using agentic AI tools to generate, test, and deploy payloads.

“Most of these are early or experimental, and Microsoft’s own assessment is that the capability ‘remain[s] limited by reliability, latency, and operational risk,’” says Igor Lasic, SVP of engineering at ReversingLabs.

But this most recent case involving Midnight Blizzard is the “clearest one on record,” according to Lasic, because two independent sources described the same infrastructure: Microsoft on July 31 as CaptiveCrunch, naming the files CornFlake and ChocoShell, and Anthropic on Sept. 10 with visibility into how the operator used Claude.

“We held both files from July 6 and July 10, before either report,” says Lasic.

Persistent limitations

Still, ReversingLabs’ recent report may reflect only the current state of the art of AI-assisted malware rebuilding, as some of the limitations that characterized the Midnight Blizzard instance could be something more advanced models might overcome, Lasic concedes.

“Today a model rewrites the file for free but cannot cheaply rewrite the server code that parses the beacon, re-register domains or re-phish victims, so the indicators that survived were the ones that had to change in two places at once,” Lasic explains. “A more capable agent with access to the whole operation could coordinate those changes, and I expect infrastructure indicators to age faster over the next few years, the way hashes already have.”

While cost and the availability of more sophisticated models is perhaps only a temporary limit for AI-assisted malware rebuilding, two other limits are closer to fundamental: the behavior of malicious code and clues left behind during a malicious campaign that enable detection.

“An implant that steals credentials has to read the credential store and one that calls home has to open a connection, whatever built it,” says Lasic. “Obfuscation makes that harder to extract, but no rewrite removes a requirement without removing the capability.”

Furthermore, a model can change the next build but not the builds already observed, timestamped and linked to the same server.

“Rebuilding faster produces more artefacts, and each one is another thread back to the operation,” Lasic concludes.

Huntress’ Bernstein backs ReversingLabs assessment that behavior-based hunting will remain effective against even AI-assisted malware development.

“You can disguise malicious code all day, but if a script tries to dump credentials or establish persistence, most modern EDRs [endpoint detection and response tools] will detect the action itself,” says Bernstein.

Another limitation of AI-assisted malware development is that even the latest models are trained to abuse known security vulnerabilities.

“They [AI models] remix known patterns rather than dreaming up zero-days,” Bernstein concludes. “Future models might get better if they can actively test their output against live environments to find undiscovered flaws, but for now, they are just recycling known techniques at a higher speed.”

item.title: Cyberattack AIs must be trained only on air-gapped systems, hundreds of AI researchers say
item.description:
Current security procedures for training AI models are inadequate, hundreds of AI researchers have warned governments and the AI community. They are calling for tougher rules and the establishment of a new international body overseeing best practice for AI development.

In an open letter the AI specialists — 487, at time of publication, including many senior academics — called for more AI safety research and greater emphasis on containment technologies.

“Strong sandboxing mechanisms including air-gapping (disconnecting from the internet) should be used to provide high-assurance containment of cyber-capable AI models,” say the signatories, who include such luminaries as Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio.

The experts said that a new international body, to be set up in consultation with governments and a wide range of AI and security specialists, could set new safety standards but also act as an organization to which containment failures could be reported, improving transparency for learning and accountability purposes.

The scientists’ demands go further than some recent calls for greater regulation of AI. Earlier this week, Microsoft president Brad Smith said AI is less regulated than washing machines or milk, although he made no firm proposals to rectify the situation. And the UK parliament is looking at ways to improve AI security, although any moves will be hampered by disagreement among AI businesses. 

Hinton and Bengio are no strangers to this kind of scientist-led initiative. In October last year, they signed an open letter warning of the dangers of developing super-intelligent AI. The letter appears not to have affected AI’s breakneck development; it remains to be seen whether AI players in boardrooms will heed the warning.

item.title: Bank of America spent millions on anti-money-laundering tech, but not enough to avoid a $1.2B fine
item.description:
Bank of America has had to spend big on IT in response to an AI security audit and findings that its anti-money-laundering (AML) controls were lacking.

The bank was fined a whopping $1.2 billion for money laundering offences this week, after banking authorities identified a lax attitude to compliance.

“We understand the seriousness of compliance, and we are responsible for getting it right,” Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan said on a conference call to discuss the company’s third-quarter financial results. “We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime,” he said, adding that “a couple hundred million” of that spending in the third quarter was on “remediation for the AML”.

The IT team had to spend a similar amount on fixing software vulnerabilities in its systems, a task that also required it to hire 1,000 consultants, Moynihan said.

The bank’s security vulnerabilities were revealed after the company received an early release of Claude Mythos Preview. In a report to the US House of Representatives Financial Services Committee, Anthropic said that Claude Mythos Preview “has already found thousands of high-severity vulnerabilities, including some in every major operating system and web browser.”

item.title: Xbow spent $40K on AI and cracked Google Chrome wide open
item.description:
A chain of vulnerabilities in Google’s Chrome browser could have enabled researchers to take control of one billion Windows machines worldwide — and it cost them just $40,000 in AI compute time to discover it.

Researchers at Xbow USA worked for six days on developing the exploit, which earned them a $250,000 bug bounty from Google, the first under the new 2026 rules.

They chose OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol for the task to demonstrate what’s possible with a publicly available model rather than a specialist security implementation. They used it to search Chrome’s source code, test ideas, and build proofs of concept, while they set the strategy, chose where to look, and checked its work.

They successfully chained together a vulnerability to escape first from the sandbox containing the V8 JavaScript engine and then from Chrome’s operating-system process sandbox, launching a Windows app from within a malicious web page.

Xbow presented its findings to Google, which fixed the flaws. The researchers set out all the details as to how the exploit was developed in a blog.

This article first appeared on Computerworld.

item.title: Hallucinated domain in official OpenAI skill underscores AI supply chain risks
item.description:
Researchers have discovered a first-of-its-kind supply-chain vulnerability in OpenAI’s official skills repository.

OpenAI maintains an official GitHub repository of skills that teach AI agents how to work with various platforms and services. As an official skill, these components are often given an implicit level of trust because they are contributed or vetted by verified vendors.

Snags arose because one OpenAI skill — designed to teach agents the best way to deploy applications on Render — instructed production apps to send their tokens to an unregistered domain (render-internal.com).

Discovering this flaw, researchers from AIR Security’s Research Lab registered the domain and pointed it at a passive (listening-only) sinkhole, which started receiving tokens and API calls from real production apps.

Testing the skill with Codex confirmed that the domain made its way into real application code as the default option.

AIR Security informed OpenAI and Render of the issue, which was resolved in mid-August, allowing its researchers to publish a technical write-up of the flaw. The issue was introduced with a commit in January.

Render removed every render-internal.com reference from the skill while OpenAI purged the Render plugin from openai/plugins. The domain was also transferred to Render’s safe holding.

The curated skill contained a hallucinated domain that deployed applications treated as a trusted internal service, putting their secrets within reach of whoever registered it.

Supply chain risk

If researchers hadn’t stumbled across Render skill flaw first, attackers might have abused a domain nobody bothered to buy to run a supply chain attack.

Niv Hoffman, AIR Security’s co-founder and CTO, said the incident shows that even official, vendor-published AI skills can contain mistakes, unsafe assumptions, dependencies, or vulnerabilities that can lead to exfiltration of secret tokens.

“Skills should be vetted and monitored like any other part of the software supply chain, so they can be patched or revoked when a vulnerability is found in one of them,” Hoffman said.

Attackers are increasingly exploring new ways of manipulating AI instruction files such as skills toward malicious ends, while also seeking AI credentials to steal or misuse to operationalize their own use of AI.

A recent Trojanized AI skill that typosquatted popular AI-related services Paperclip and Browser Use on open agent skills ecosystem skills.sh garnered 1.7M installations in a scheme to instruct agents to install a credential stealer from GitHub instead.
